name: LT6657BHMS8-4.096#PBF
title: 1.5ppm/°C low noise buffered voltage reference
summary: The LT6657 is a curvature-compensated bandgap series reference with a buffered output that sources and sinks 10mA, in 1.25V, 2.5V, 3V, 4.096V and 5V versions. It holds 0.1% initial accuracy, a temperature coefficient of 1.5ppm/°C (A grade) or 3ppm/°C (B grade) maximum, and 0.5ppmP-P noise from 0.1Hz to 10Hz. It runs from 50mV above its output up to 40V, survives a reversed supply or output, limits short-circuit current, shuts down thermally and drops below 4µA with SHDN low. It can also be wired as a positive or negative shunt reference. Specified from –40°C to 125°C in an 8-lead MSOP.
key_figures: A grade 1.5ppm/°C max, B grade 3ppm/°C max
VOUT + 50mV to 40V; 1.5V min for the 1.25V option
reverse supply, reverse output, output current limit, thermal shutdown

notes: The letter after LT6657 is the grade: A is 1.5ppm/°C, B is 3ppm/°C maximum. The suffix after MS8 is the output voltage.
A and B parts of one voltage carry the same marking; the grade is on a label on the shipping container.
Some packages also come in 500-unit reels with the suffix #TRMPBF.
PBF parts are RoHS and WEEE compliant.

pins.name: DNC
pins.function: Wired inside the part to internal functions. Leave floating, keep leakage from it as low as possible and keep other routing clear of it.

pins.name: VIN
pins.function: Supply input. Needs a 0.1µF or larger capacitor (1µF for the 1.25V option) to GND close to the pin.

pins.name: SHDN
pins.function: Shutdown, active low: pulled low it turns the part off and the supply current falls below 2µA. Drive it from outside; for normal operation take it to a logic high or to VIN, and tie it to VIN if it is not used.

pins.name: GND
pins.function: Ground. It carries the supply return current, so its trace impedance matters; connect it to a quiet ground plane, best as a star point shared with the circuits that use the reference.

pins.name: VOUT
pins.function: Reference output; sources or sinks load current. Needs at least 1µF (2.7µF for the 1.25V option) for stability.

Note 4: Temperature coefficient is the largest change of output voltage divided by the specified temperature span.
Note 5: Both regulation figures come from pulsed tests across the listed ranges of VIN or IOUT; any shift caused by the die warming up is extra and is added on its own.

Note 6: The P-P noise figure is taken through a 2-pole 0.1Hz highpass and a 3-pole 10Hz lowpass, for 10 seconds, with the part in still air so lead thermocouples do not add to it. Because noise is random, repeated 10 second readings scatter; over 1000 such intervals some read above a single typical interval. The typical figure is one a typical unit stays under in more than half of the 1000 intervals (Application Note 124 gives the test). RMS noise comes from a spectrum analyzer, with the part shielded.

Note 7: Long-term drift slows roughly logarithmically: the shift after the first 1000 hours is much smaller, the second thousand hours normally giving under a third of the first, and less after that. Assembly stress from the board acting on the IC also changes it.

Note 8: Thermal hysteresis comes from mechanical stress that depends on the temperature the part saw before. The output is always read at 25°C, after a cycle from 25°C to cold and back or to hot and back; the figure is the largest change between the averages of three hot or three cold cycles, after one cold and one hot preconditioning cycle. Kept within 30 degrees of its working temperature, an instrument usually sees little error from it.

circuits.title: Basic connection
circuits.description: The plain series reference. The supply, anywhere from 50mV above the output up to 40V, goes to VIN, and SHDN is tied to it so the part is always on. A 0.1µF capacitor bypasses the input and a 1µF capacitor on VOUT keeps the output buffer stable.

circuits.title: Transient load test circuit
circuits.description: The set-up for the load-step captures. The reference runs from 3V with SHDN tied to VIN; a signal generator drives the output node through 1kΩ, so stepping the generator voltage steps the current the reference sources or sinks.

circuits.title: Positive shunt mode operation
circuits.description: The reference as a two-terminal positive shunt. VIN, SHDN and VOUT are joined and fed from VDD through RSHUNT; the node is +VOUT and carries COUT of 1µF or more to ground. RSHUNT comes from the shunt equation. Not for the 1.25V option.

circuits.title: Negative shunt mode operation
circuits.description: The shunt connection as a negative reference. VIN, SHDN and VOUT go to ground, and the GND pin is the –VOUT node, fed from –VDD through RSHUNT, with COUT of 1µF between the two. ISHUNT must stay above 2.5mA and IOUT_MAX under 8.5mA. Not for the 1.25V option.
notes: ISHUNT_MAX = 2.5mA + IOUT_MAX, with IOUT_MAX < 8.5mA.

circuits.title: Extended supply range reference
circuits.description: Runs the reference from a 40V to 100V supply. A 270k resistor from the supply biases a BZX84C12 12V Zener; a 2N3440 NPN with its collector on the supply and its base on the Zener feeds VIN and SHDN from its emitter, which carries 0.1µF to ground. VOUT carries 1µF.

circuits.title: Boosted output current reference
circuits.description: A 2N2905 PNP raises the output current to 300mA. The supply, at least 1.5V above VOUT, feeds the PNP emitter and, through 220Ω with 4.7µF across it, the PNP base and the reference VIN and SHDN, which carry 0.1µF to ground. The PNP collector joins VOUT, which carries 1µF.

circuits.title: Boosted output current with current limit
circuits.description: The boosted connection with a 10Ω resistor in the PNP emitter and an LED across the 220Ω resistor, for up to 100mA. The LED clamps the voltage across the 220Ω resistor and so limits the output current; it must be fitted. The supply is at least 2V above VOUT.
notes: LED1 sets the current limit: without it the 220Ω drop is not clamped and the output current is not limited.

circuits.title: Sinking current from external circuitry
circuits.description: An outside supply VEXT, above VOUT, drives current into the output through RLOAD and the reference sinks it. The reference supply runs from VOUT – 230mV to 40V, with 0.1µF on VIN and 1µF on VOUT.

circuits.title: 1.5V minimum supply voltage
circuits.description: The 1.25V option running from a 1.5V supply. It needs 1µF on the input and 2.7µF on the output, and in this connection it sources up to 5mA and sinks up to 10mA.

circuits.title: Low noise statistical averaging reference
circuits.description: Four 2.5V references run from one 3V to 40V supply, each with its own 0.1µF input and 1µF output capacitor, and join the common output through 20Ω each; the common node carries 1µF. Output noise is the noise of one part divided by the square root of the number in parallel, half for four.
notes: Output noise eNOUT = eN/√N, N the number of LT6657s in parallel.

circuits.title: Low noise precision 20-bit analog-to-digital converter application
circuits.description: The reference supplies the REF input of an LTC2378-20 20-bit SAR ADC. It runs from 5V with SHDN tied to VIN; its output carries 1µF at the pin and 47µF X7R plus 0.1µF beside the ADC, and drives both REF and REF/DGC. A dual LT6203 buffers the differential input: each half is a unity-gain follower driving IN+ or IN– through 10Ω, with 6800pF NPO from each input to ground and 3300pF NPO across the pair. The ADC runs from +2.5V (VDD) and +3.3V (OVDD), each bypassed with 10µF and 0.1µF. Measured: SNR 97dB, SINAD 97dB, THD –117dB, SFDR 120dB.
notes: U2 is one LT6203 dual op amp, V+ 8V. The first half is drawn with pin 2 on its non-inverting input, pin 3 on its inverting input and pin 1 its output; the second half with pin 5 non-inverting, pin 6 inverting and pin 7 output. U3 GND pins are 3, 6, 10 and 16; its pin 1 goes to ground through 1k.

operation.text: Line regulation is typically far under 1ppm/V: 10V more on the input moves the output about 2ppm. Load regulation in the MS8 is under 2µV/mA, so a 5mA load change moves it about 10µV; both are measured with short, low duty cycle pulses. Resistance in the VOUT and GND traces adds errors of the same size, so keep those runs short and give the load its own ground return. While sourcing, the GND pin can serve as a Kelvin sense point. Die heating adds a separate shift, given by the self-heating equations.

Put at least 0.1µF (1µF for the 1.25V option) on the input, close to the part, for supply rejection; a long, inductive input lead can ring on big load steps. The output needs at least 1µF (2.7µF for 1.25V) near the part. Its value and type set stability, turn-on time and settling. Keep its ESR under 0.5Ω, since ESR adds a zero to the buffer's response, and choose a part that still behaves above 100kHz, where capacitance falls and ESR rises. For a large output capacitance, a low-ESR ceramic in parallel with a tantalum gives a well damped response, for example 10µF ceramic (ESR under 0.5Ω) with 47µF tantalum.

X7R ceramics are small and stable over temperature but are piezoelectric: vibration turns into charge, which shows up as noise. Film capacitors have no piezo effect. Polyester, polycarbonate and polypropylene are stable over temperature, though polypropylene tops out at 85°C to 105°C and above that the working voltage must be derated. PPS film works over a wide temperature range and comes above 1µF. Film capacitor life shortens near or past rated voltage, at high temperature and with AC ripple; in a reference, ripple appears only during transients.

The output rises at a rate set by the current limit charging the output capacitor (turn-on equation). With 1µF and no load, a 0.4VP-P input step moves the output less than 1mV peak. A load on the output speeds the response; more output capacitance gives a smaller but slower response.

The output stage sources and sinks equal currents. Sourcing, it behaves as an ordinary low dropout regulator. Sinking, it stays in regulation with the input equal to, above, or a little below the output, so dropout while sinking is given as a negative VIN – VOUT: a typical unit holds with the input 250mV below the output, 50mV guaranteed (not the 1.25V option). Lower input drops it out of regulation. This is what lets the input and output be tied together for shunt use.

With VIN, SHDN and VOUT joined, the part works as a two-terminal reference, positive or negative. Keep ISHUNT above 2.5mA for the same performance as series operation; the load may take at most 8.5mA; COUT must be 1µF or more. The 1.25V option works in series mode only, and it runs from as little as 1.5V.

SHDN below 0.8V (to GND) turns the output off and the part draws about 2µA; below 0.4V it draws 0.01µA typical. The pin turns on at 1.26V and turns off about 150mV lower; logic high is 1.6V (1.45V for the 1.25V option). Drive it from logic or from an open-collector or open-drain stage with a pull-up, sized to supply the driver's leakage, usually a few µA, plus what the pin itself draws, typically under 5µA at 6V. Tie it to VIN if unused.

Dissipation depends on VIN, load current and package; the MSOP-8 has θJA = 273°C/W. The junction may go to 150°C, but for best accuracy keep its temperature change small. The maximum ambient curve assumes a 125°C junction. Above 10mA load the part may enter current limit, stop regulating and run hotter than the curve shows. Sourcing from a high input voltage, an internal thermal shutdown caps the dissipation. Sinking dissipates much less, and the sink current limit protects the part, so no thermal shutdown is needed there.

With 0.5ppmP-P from 0.1Hz to 10Hz, board design can dominate system noise. Junctions of different metals in leads and traces form thermocouples, and uneven airflow puts the leads at different temperatures, producing a thermoelectric voltage at the output; use few such junctions and limit airflow (Application Note 82). Place both capacitors near the part. DC PSRR is 130dB, but a steady supply still gives the best result. Paralleling references lowers noise by √N.

The typical 0.1Hz to 10Hz figure is one that at least half of 10 second readings fall below: the LT6657-2.5 reads under 0.5ppmP-P in at least 50% of them. Over long periods the peak can be much larger; the likely maximum is often estimated as the RMS value times a crest factor of 6 to 8.4. The part was also measured by the AN124 method, logging the output through a preamplifier and 0.1Hz to 10Hz filter into an ADC or DVM and computing peak-to-peak over hundreds of 10 second intervals: the LT6657-2.5 stays under 0.55ppmP-P in 80% of intervals and under 0.59ppmP-P in 95%.

The hysteresis histogram is taken on the LT6657-2.5. The part can dissipate a lot: at 40V in with 5mA sourced the 2.5V part dissipates 244mW, raising the die 73°C in the MSOP-8, which can take the junction past 125°C and shift the output by thermal hysteresis at each power-up.
Drift data come from parts soldered to boards as in use, held in an oven at TA = 35°C and read regularly with an 8.5 digit DVM.

operation.topic: Board stress and IR reflow shift
operation.text: Soldering to a board stresses the part and can shift the output and change the die temperature coefficient; the board influences every kind of stability, over time, after temperature cycles and with humidity (AN82). The heat of IR or convection reflow shifts the output too, because the die and package materials expand and contract at different rates and the stress on the die moves; the shift resembles thermal hysteresis but is larger. The reflow shift histogram shows the reflow effect alone, without board mechanical stress, after a 260°C peak lead-free profile.
